newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook - Gasoline leads upside move.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook - Gasoline leads upside move.

text.p: Midwest gasoline is expected to hold and even build on price gains seen last week amid concerns delays in gasoline scheduling on the Explorer Pipeline will keep inventories tight, traders said.

In New York Harbor, expectations for below average gasoline imports were expected to keep prices firm and spur a new round of strength on the Gulf Coast, where a number of refinery problems already fueled strength last week.
On the West Coast, a six-week downtrend apears to have run its course, with traders in the region expecting gasoline to lead the upside reversal.
- MIDCONTINENT

Differentials on midcontinent conventional unleaded gasoline widened two cents a gallon late last week on the concerns, to offers of 4.25 cents above June NYMEX futures in Group Three and 2.75 cents over in Chicago.

Midcontinent traders said they were concerned that delays would prevent 14th-cycle Explorer Pipeline shipments originating in Texas from reaching their Williams Pipeline relay point in Tulsa, Oklahoma, by the end of the month.

"Some people are caught short and if the Explorer gasoline doesn't make it (to Tulsa) by the end of the month, it's too late" to get barrels into the Williams Pipeline link for June deliveries into the Midwest, one player said.
"We were looking for it to arrive by May 23 but it probably won't arrive until June 2 or 3," the Chicago broker said, noting Midwest gasoline stocks are 3.4 million barrels below last year.

"If you market on the Williams, you have to have supply in hand by the beginning of the month you want to ship," another trader noted, predicting a "bidding war" for barrels could ensue as last week's short-covering continues.
Explorer shipping cycles are based upon 10-day periods -- three per month -- with the delivery time from Texas to Tulsa taking about five days.

Sources said the Explorer has been running from five to 10 days behind schedule for about a month on gasoline shipments to the Midwest and is shipping less gasoline pipeline in order send more distillates.
- NEW YORK HARBOR
Gasoline prices in New York Harbor (NYH) were expected to remain in balance amid talk of a near-term drop in imports from Europe and South America, industry sources said.
"There are fewer imports coming in during the second half of May than in the previous two months. They'll probably taper off between now and the end of the month," said one trader who tracks imports.
The relief on the import front comes right at the time when Tosco Corp is set to reopen its refinery near Philadelphia, traders and analysts said.

Industry sources, generally bullish on gasoline demand this year, have been saying the scheduled reopening of Tosco's Trainer refinery in mid-May has kept a lid on upward movement of prices in energy markets, and imports could crush them.

"I think we'll see good strength on gasoline demand. I'm cautiously optimistic for refiners this year," said Cyrus Tahmasebbi, an economist and president of Energy Trends Inc, a Bethesda, Maryland consultancy.
"The only thing I'm worried about is imports," Tahmasebbi continued. "Once the margins get good, here come the imports."
The 473,000 bpd in gasoline imports recorded by the American Petroleum Institute (API) in the week ended May 2, is likely to be on the high side for the month.

One European trader said the steep backwardation in the gasoline market, with prompt barrels trading at a premium to barrels for delivery later in the month, means that currently barrels must be loaded by May 20th.

Regular reformulated gasoline was showing some of that tightness, with prompt differentials pegged at 1.30 cents over June NYMEX unleaded futures, and deferred barrels at considerably weaker levels, traders said.
Traders said the expected slowdown in import activity in the second half of the month puts the onus on U.S. Gulf Coast refineries to make up the difference.
"We'll probably have to draw more from the Gulf Coast," the cargo trader said.
- GULF COAST
Gasoline prices on the Gulf Coast, where traders have been reporting sundry problems, are already expected to be strong in the coming week or two, traders said.
The added pull related to solid demand on the East Coast amid lower import levels will keep the heat on prices and likely push them higher, traders said.
"Differentials could get stronger here because of the pull from New York," a Gulf Coast trader said.
Prompt regular unleaded gasoline differentials stood at 3.75 cents under June futures on Monday afternoon -- about where they were Friday, and a touch firmer than a week ago.
- WEST COAST
West Coast spot product prices were expected to firm this week, traders said, with summertime driving demand reversing a six-week decline for spot gasoline.
"There's not much downside left here. It's really crashed," one Los Angeles-based broker said.
Spot CARB gasoline prices were pegged at 63.50 cents a gallon Friday, down from 86 cents in late March, according to the California Energy Commision.
Prices have fallen as refineries cranked up production after wintertime shutdowns for maintenance and repairs.
Last week's inventory report from trade group American Petroleum Institute (API), showed refinery use up 3.1 percentage points, to 94.9 percent of capacity.
-- New York Energy Desk, 1 212 859 1620
